Lesson: Four-Chord Loops

A great many songs are one loop of four chords, played round and round while the melody, the words and the arrangement change on top. The loops are not very different from each other: they are the same handful of chords (I, ii, IV, V, vi, and a few borrowed from the minor) in a different order, or with one of them swapped. This lesson goes through the loops one at a time. Each has the chords, the same four bars on a grand staff (block chords in the treble, the bass note below) and the site’s backing band, which plays it round and round so that you hear it as a loop.

How to use the page. Press ▶ on any chart and the band plays four times round after a one-bar count-in. The bar that is sounding lights up, on the chart and on the staff. Under every chord is its Roman numeral, which stays the same in every key: C G Am F in the key of C is the same loop as D A Bm G in the key of D. The strip at the bottom of the window sets the key, the feel, the tempo and the chord instrument, and you can change them while the band plays. The shaded bars are the ones that differ from the first loop.

1. The axis loop: I V vi IV

C, G, Am, F. The loop that is under Let It Be, No Woman, No Cry and the verse of Don’t Stop Believin’, among a great many others. The bass drops from C to G, rises a step to A and falls a third to F. Three major chords and one minor: the minor chord keeps it from sounding simply happy.

Play it until you can hum the bass note of each bar. Every other loop is compared with this one.

2. The same chords, started later: vi IV I V

Am, F, C, G. The four chords are the same; the loop starts on the minor chord, so that it sounds like a minor song, and the major chord C arrives in the middle. Zombie by the Cranberries is this loop (in E minor), and so is the chorus of Despacito.

Compare the two charts: there is no new chord. Where a loop starts is what the ear takes for home. The other two starting points are IV I V vi (F, C, G, Am) and V vi IV I (G, Am, F, C).

3. The fifties loop: I vi IV V

C, Am, F, G. The doo-wop loop. It has the chords of the axis loop, but with the minor chord second, so the bass steps down by thirds: C, A, F, and then the G climbs to C again. Stand by Me is built on it. Listen to bar 4: the V chord is the last bar and it leads straight back to C.

4. The turnaround: I vi ii V

C, Am, Dm, G. Replace the IV with its relative minor, ii. The bass now moves round the circle of fifths: C, A, D, G, and back to C. This is the turnaround of jazz, and the A section of Gershwin’s I Got Rhythm (the “rhythm changes”) begins this way. Put a seventh on each chord and it is the sound of a standard.

Bar 3 is the only difference from the fifties loop. The ii chord and the IV chord share two of their three notes (F and A), so one can stand in for the other.

5. Out and back: I IV V IV

C, F, G, F. The loop of Louie Louie and Wild Thing. There is no minor chord and no change of direction; the loop goes up to the dominant and back down by the same step. Because the bar-4 chord is IV, not I, it does not feel finished, and the loop goes round again and again.

6. Borrowing a chord: I ♭VII IV I

C, B♭, F, C. B♭ is not in the key of C. It is the chord on the flat seventh, borrowed from the mixolydian mode (a major scale with a flat seventh) and the note that the blues calls the flat seven. Sweet Home Alabama goes I, ♭VII, IV this way. In C the bass goes down a step, then down a fourth, then down a fourth again.

7. The minor loops

Two loops in the minor, written here in C minor (three flats in the signature).

  • i ♭VII ♭VI V: Cm, B♭, A♭, G. The Andalusian loop. The bass falls by step, C, B♭, A♭, G, and the last chord is a major V, with the leading tone B, so that it pulls hard back to Cm. Hit the Road Jack is this loop.
  • i ♭VI ♭III ♭VII: Cm, A♭, E♭, B♭. The four chords of the axis loop in E♭ major, started on the vi chord: loop 2 in its minor key. It is the sound of much current pop.

Play the two minor loops and then loop 2. The notes are different, but the shape, down by steps then up by a third, is the same.

Build your own loop

Choose a chord for each bar, or start from one of the loops above, and the chart and the staff rewrite themselves. Change a menu while the band is playing and the new chords come in at the next bar. The numeral next to each chord is its place in the key of C.

Test your ear

The band plays one of the loops. Pick the one you heard. If you are not sure, listen for the bass first: does it fall, climb or leap?

Where to go next

  • Play along. Set the strip at the bottom to Loop, pick a key and play or sing a melody over each loop in turn. Start with just the chord roots.
  • Take a loop you built to Tools → Backing Track (use Copy as ABC above and paste it into Edit the changes (ABC) there) to choose the bass line, comping rhythm and drum groove.
  • Try the moves of the lesson on C, Am, F, G (extensions, passing chords, secondary dominants, two-fives) on any of these loops.
